tests.s: A coach tells his players, "You're either fully committed to this team, or you don't care about it at all."
A phone salesperson tells Jamal, "You either buy our top model, or you settle for a phone that can't do anything useful."

why: Test 2 ('or leave your family unprotected') is also a fear appeal, and appeal to emotion is a wrong option; replaced with an emotion-free either/or
Concluding from two personal encounters is also 'relying on isolated examples' (anecdotal evidence def); both tests fit it
Tests have the person ignoring large studies in favor of one story (reads as cherry-picking) and the neighbor's 'it cured me' is a causal inference from one case
Five dentists / 15 voters can be read as 'isolated examples instead of systematic data'
Test 1 draws a broad conclusion from one unrepresentative month, which also matches hasty generalization and small sample
Test 1 (talking about crushed parents instead of the grade) is also an irrelevant topic brought in to distract

tests.s: Parents assume the school's star athlete must also be honest and hardworking, though they know nothing else about him.
Impressed by how attractive and well-spoken a job candidate is, the interviewer assumes he must also be organized and good with numbers.

why: Test 2 was about a company's phones, but def says 'a person's unrelated qualities'; replaced with a person-based scenario

set.scenario: Kwame refuses a coin-flip bet in which he would win $120 on heads and lose $100 on tails, even though on average he would come out ahead.

why: 'the odds favor him' is false: a fair coin is even odds; it is the expected value that favors him
Test 2 treats a doctor and an online forum as equally credible, which also reads as false equivalence
Test 1 describes a trial where half got an inactive pill (that half is a control group), and headaches improving on their own is regression/natural recovery

tests.s: Jamal says the town's popular spring festival is worthless today because it was first started decades ago to promote a local car dealership.
Sofia won't try a popular dish because it was invented by accident when a cook made a mistake, so she says it "can't be any good."

why: Old test 1 ('nice' once meant 'foolish') turns on two meanings of one word, so equivocation (a wrong option) fits as well
Status quo bias is commonly explained by loss aversion; learners can defensibly pick it for sticking with the current account/default
Test 2 (teacher decides the student 'stopped trying') attributes the drop to her character, which matches fundamental attribution error

tests.s: A brochure says a new bike helmet "cuts your chance of a head injury by 50%," but the fine print shows it fell from 2 in 10,000 rides to 1 in 10,000.
A news story warns that a snack raises the risk of a rare cancer by 30%, without mentioning that the lifetime risk goes from 10 in 100,000 to 13 in 100,000.

why: Def is about 'chance of harm' but test 1 was about the chance of clear skin; replaced with a harm example. Base-rate neglect also fits ignoring the tiny baseline ('rare cancer')
Test 1 (degree required -> has degree -> sure to be hired) is formally affirming the consequent

tests.s: "If the dog ate the cake, there will be crumbs on the floor. There are crumbs on the floor, so the dog must have eaten the cake."
"If the battery is dead, the car won't start. Wei's car won't start, so the battery must be dead."

why: Premise 'if someone has the flu, they have a fever' is medically false (flu often occurs without fever); also the underlying error is treating a necessary condition as sufficient, so that option fits too
Tests treat a sufficient condition (snow, studying abroad) as necessary, so necessary vs. sufficient also fits
